10 questions across 5 topic areas, approximately 30 minutes

Both authors co-authored the studies discussed: Che in PRIMETEST and Papachristofilou in SAKK 01/10 [Q]. Where the article and EAU 2026 differ, the correct answer follows the guideline; these questions carry ⚠.

A: Marker-negative node below 2 cm: repeat cross-sectional imaging after 6–8 weeks before any treatment [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
Stage IIA/B means retroperitoneal involvement without distant metastases and markers no higher than S1 (LDH below 1.5 times the upper normal limit, β-hCG below 5000 mIU/ml) [Q].
Supradiaphragmatic lesions exclude radiotherapy and IIA/B de-escalation: chemotherapy according to IGCCCG [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.6.1].
B: Chemotherapy: three cycles of BEP, or four cycles of EP if bleomycin is contraindicated [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
Radiotherapy: para-aortic plus ipsilateral pelvic fields, 30 Gy in stage IIA and 36 Gy in stage IIB; 27 Gy increases the relapse rate [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
Both standards cure more than 90%, but carry late toxicity including second malignancies (2% after radiotherapy, 4% after chemotherapy in one review) [Q].
C: Primary RPLND is an alternative with conditions: selection, experienced surgeon, specialist centre, preferably a study [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.1].
Modified unilateral template according to the side of disease; antegrade ejaculation preserved in 94% in PRIMETEST [Q].
Open and robotic approaches are both feasible and safe; no randomised comparison, robotic surgery requires expertise [Q].
D: Risk markers after RPLND: more than two positive nodes or nodes above 3 cm [Q].
Then consider one adjuvant cycle of BEP; PRIMETEST II is examining which factors justify it [Q].
Relapse after RPLND is chemotherapy-naive: first-line treatment according to IGCCCG, not a second-line regimen [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.4].
E: SAKK 01/10: one cycle of carboplatin AUC 7, then involved-node radiotherapy; volume approximately one quarter of the dog-leg field [Q].
3-year PFS 93.7%, narrowly missing the primary endpoint of 95%; not for routine use according to EAU [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2].
Relapses occurred almost exclusively in stage IIB; SAKK 01/18 is testing one cycle of EP and 30 Gy in that setting, results 2026/2027 [Q].

questions.objective: Can distinguish follow-up imaging from immediate treatment for a marker-negative, borderline enlarged retroperitoneal lymph node.
questions.reference: Article: case example, background, implications for practice; EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1
questions.vignette: A 42-year-old man has been on active surveillance for 12 months after left inguinal orchiectomy (seminoma pT1, 42 mm, without rete testis invasion). Follow-up CT shows a new single left para-aortic lymph node with a transverse diameter of just under 1 cm. AFP, β-hCG and LDH are normal; he has no symptoms. The tumour board must decide the next step.
questions.lead: What is appropriate for this finding?

opts.A: Start immediate chemotherapy with three cycles of BEP
opts.B: Give a single dose of carboplatin AUC 7 as delayed adjuvant treatment
opts.C: Para-aortic and ipsilateral pelvic radiotherapy with 30 Gy
opts.D: Wait for repeat cross-sectional imaging after about eight weeks
opts.E: Continue routine follow-up at the previously planned interval

rat.A: Misconception: every new lymph node is a relapse. Without marker elevation, reactive enlargement is possible [Q]; on average about 10% of these nodes are not metastatic [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
rat.B: Misconception: the adjuvant concept for stage I can be applied to a possible relapse. Carboplatin monotherapy is not a standard option in stage IIA/B [Q].
rat.C: Misconception: small finding, small treatment. Radiotherapy is standard for confirmed stage IIA [Q]; here it would treat an unconfirmed finding.
rat.D: Repeat cross-sectional imaging after about 8 weeks confirms or refutes the stage [Q]; treatment starts only with growth, marker rise or biopsy confirmation [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
rat.E: Misconception: a new finding does not change the follow-up schedule. It requires a targeted, earlier check instead of the routine interval [Q].

questions.core: A marker-negative node below 2 cm does not establish stage IIA [Q]. Only interval imaging distinguishes reactive enlargement from metastasis and determines whether treatment is needed at all.
questions.ev: The authors recommend repeating cross-sectional imaging after about 8 weeks in stage IIA without marker elevation [Q]. EAU specifies 6–8 weeks and starts treatment only when metastasis is unequivocal through biopsy, increase in size or number, or marker rise [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1]. In the article's case example, the node had grown to 23 mm after 2 months [Q].
questions.prax: Immediate treatment overtreats some patients and exposes them to the late toxicity of standard procedures. The imaging interval should therefore be explicitly recorded in the tumour board decision [X].
questions.merk: Marker-negative and below 2 cm: repeat imaging after 6–8 weeks first, then decide on treatment.

questions.objective: Recognises that supradiaphragmatic disease excludes infradiaphragmatic radiotherapy and the de-escalation concepts tested for IIA/B.
questions.vignette: A 33-year-old man with pure seminoma undergoes staging after orchiectomy. CT shows a 2.6 cm left para-aortic lymph node and an additional 1.4 cm left supraclavicular node; the lungs and visceral organs are unremarkable. AFP is normal; β-hCG and LDH are mildly elevated, within S1. He would prefer to avoid chemotherapy. Initial treatment must be selected.
questions.lead: Which approach is indicated for this extent of disease?

opts.A: Hockey-stick radiotherapy with 36 Gy and a supraclavicular boost
opts.B: Cisplatin-based chemotherapy according to the IGCCCG prognostic group
opts.C: Carboplatin AUC 7, then involved-node radiotherapy to both lesions
opts.D: Primary RPLND and excision of the supraclavicular node
opts.E: Para-aortic radiotherapy with 36 Gy and observation of the supraclavicular node

rat.A: Misconception: the field can be extended to supradiaphragmatic lesions. Conventional radiotherapy is a local infradiaphragmatic concept; it is inappropriate with a supraclavicular metastasis [Q].
rat.B: With the supraclavicular node, disease is no longer locoregional [Q]. Seminomas from stage IIC onwards receive primary chemotherapy according to IGCCCG [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.6.1].
rat.C: Misconception: SAKK 01/10 applies to any low tumour burden. The regimen was tested only in stage IIA/B [Q] and is not established for routine use even there [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2].
rat.D: Misconception: surgical de-escalation applies to any nodal site. Primary RPLND was studied for retroperitoneal involvement in stage IIA/B [Q], not supradiaphragmatic spread.
rat.E: Misconception: the smaller lesion can be ignored. The authors specifically cite this scenario to explain why local radiotherapy without complete staging fails [Q].

questions.core: Stage determines the treatment principle. With the supraclavicular node, disease is no longer locoregional, and all local or de-escalated IIA/B concepts lose their basis.
questions.ev: Stage IIA/B means retroperitoneal nodal metastases without distant metastases and markers no higher than S1 [Q]. Infradiaphragmatic radiotherapy is local and inappropriate with an additional supraclavicular metastasis [Q]. For seminomas from stage IIC onwards, EAU recommends primary chemotherapy according to IGCCCG, BEP x 3 for good prognosis [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.6.1].
questions.prax: Before any radiotherapy or de-escalation, staging must include the chest and supraclavicular region; the case example therefore used CT of the trunk [Q]. A wish to avoid chemotherapy does not change the indication here [X].
questions.merk: Supraclavicular node in seminoma: not stage II; chemotherapy according to IGCCCG instead of radiotherapy.

questions.objective: Can choose the equivalent chemotherapy regimen in stage IIA/B when bleomycin is contraindicated.
questions.vignette: A 45-year-old man with stage IIA seminoma (single para-aortic node 1.8 cm, growth confirmed on repeat imaging, normal markers) chooses chemotherapy after counselling about all options. The respiratory team explicitly advises against bleomycin because of pre-existing lung disease. The chemotherapy regimen must be selected.
questions.lead: Which regimen is appropriate for this patient?

opts.A: Three cycles of BEP at standard doses
opts.B: Three cycles of EP without another cycle
opts.C: Four cycles of VIP with G-CSF prophylaxis
opts.D: One cycle of carboplatin at AUC 7

rat.A: Misconception: the standard regimen applies regardless of contraindications. The article and EAU explicitly provide an alternative for patients unsuitable for bleomycin [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
rat.B: Misconception: bleomycin can simply be omitted. The article specifies four cycles of EP as the alternative [Q]; the extra cycle compensates for its omission [X].
rat.C: Misconception: confusion of prognostic groups. VIP is the bleomycin-free alternative in the intermediate-prognosis group [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.3.1.2], not in stage IIA.
rat.D: Misconception: applying stage I adjuvant therapy. Carboplatin monotherapy is not a standard option in stage IIA/B [Q].
rat.E: Four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin replace three cycles of BEP when bleomycin is contraindicated [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].

questions.core: A contraindication to bleomycin changes the regimen, not the treatment principle: four cycles of EP instead of three cycles of BEP.
questions.ev: Guideline-concordant treatment in stage IIA/B is three cycles of BEP, alternatively four cycles of EP when bleomycin is contraindicated, or radiotherapy [Q]. EAU also specifies BEP x 3 or EP x 4 when there are concerns about bleomycin, and reports relapse rates of 0–8% for chemotherapy in stage IIA [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
questions.prax: The pulmonary history must inform regimen selection before treatment; overlooking it introduces avoidable lung risk [X]. Counselling must also cover the late cardiovascular and renal toxicity of cisplatin treatment and second malignancies [Q].
questions.merk: Bleomycin contraindicated: four cycles of EP instead of three cycles of BEP.

questions.objective: Can define the guideline-concordant radiotherapy field and dose for stage IIA.
questions.vignette: A 38-year-old man with stage IIA seminoma (single para-aortic node 1.6 cm, growth confirmed on repeat imaging, normal markers, otherwise normal staging from chest to pelvis) declines chemotherapy and surgery. He chooses radiotherapy. Target volume and dose must be defined.
questions.lead: Which radiotherapy concept follows the guideline?

opts.A: Para-aortic and ipsilateral pelvic fields, total dose 30 Gy
opts.B: Para-aortic and ipsilateral pelvic fields, total dose 36 Gy
opts.C: Para-aortic and ipsilateral pelvic fields, total dose 27 Gy
opts.D: Para-aortic only, without a pelvic field, total dose 30 Gy
opts.E: Involved-node only, without carboplatin, total dose 30 Gy

rat.A: The conventional field covers retroperitoneal and ipsilateral pelvic lymphatic drainage, with 30 Gy in stage IIA [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
rat.B: Misconception: confusion of stages. 36 Gy is the dose for stage IIB [Q]; in stage IIA it means a higher dose without proven added benefit [X].
rat.C: Misconception: less dose only reduces toxicity. A reduced dose of 27 Gy in stage IIA is associated with a higher relapse rate [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
rat.D: Misconception: a para-aortic-only field is sufficient in metastatic disease. Ipsilateral pelvic lymphatic drainage is part of the standard field in stage IIA [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: small-volume radiotherapy is a stand-alone treatment. In SAKK 01/10 it always followed one cycle of carboplatin [Q]; alone it lacks activity outside the field [X].

questions.core: Radiotherapy is a standard option alongside chemotherapy in stage IIA: para-aortic and ipsilateral pelvic fields, dose 30 Gy [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
questions.ev: The article specifies 30 Gy for stage IIA and 36 Gy for IIB with para-aortic and ipsilateral pelvic irradiation [Q]. EAU recommends the same doses, reports 5-year relapse-free survival of 92% in stage IIA and a higher relapse rate after reduction to 27 Gy [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].
questions.prax: The large field of approximately 1200 cm³ increases the risk of second malignancies [Q]; EAU requires counselling about late effects of both options [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.6.1]. Complete staging is essential because radiotherapy acts only locally [Q].
questions.merk: Stage IIA: para-aortic plus ipsilateral pelvic irradiation with 30 Gy, not 27 Gy or 36 Gy.

questions.objective: Can classify primary RPLND for IIA/B seminoma as an alternative with conditions and explain relapse risk.
questions.reference: Article: evidence, conclusions on RPLND; EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.1
questions.vignette: A 30-year-old man with stage IIA seminoma (single node 1.9 cm, growth confirmed on repeat imaging, normal markers) wants neither chemotherapy nor radiotherapy and asks about retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. The hospital is a testicular cancer centre with RPLND expertise. Counselling precedes the tumour board decision.
questions.lead: How should primary RPLND be classified for this patient?

opts.A: Established standard with the same relapse-free outcome as chemotherapy
opts.B: Contraindicated in seminoma because only systemic treatment is curative
opts.C: Alternative at an expert centre, ideally within studies
opts.D: Useful only as residual tumour resection after chemotherapy
opts.E: Equivalent if routinely followed by three cycles of BEP

rat.A: Misconception: inclusion in guidelines means equivalence. Relapse-free survival in the studies was 70–90% [Q]; EAU notes a lack of longer follow-up and comparative studies [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.1].
rat.B: A misconception dating from before the prospective studies. SEMS, COTRIMS and PRIMETEST tested primary RPLND in stage IIA/B [Q]; it is not contraindicated.
rat.C: The article and EAU require patient selection, surgical quality and a specialist centre for primary RPLND; according to EAU, ideally within a study or prospective cohort [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.1].
rat.D: Misconception: confusion with post-chemotherapy resection. This is primary RPLND as an alternative to chemotherapy [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: routine further treatment secures the result. It defeats the purpose; only a single adjuvant cycle of BEP is considered when risk markers are present [Q].

questions.core: Primary RPLND is a potentially curative alternative without chemotherapy or radiotherapy, but only under conditions: a selected patient, an experienced surgeon and a specialist centre.
questions.ev: In SEMS, COTRIMS and PRIMETEST, relapse-free survival was 70–90%; all relapses were successfully treated with chemotherapy [Q]. NCCN guidelines (Version 2.2025) list primary RPLND as an option for stage IIA/B seminomas below 3 cm [Q]. EAU describes 2-year relapse rates of 5–30% and recommends the procedure only by highly experienced surgeons in specialist centres, ideally within a prospective cohort or study [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.1].
questions.prax: Counselling must explain the higher relapse risk compared with standard treatments and the chemotherapy then required [Q]. The indication belongs in an interdisciplinary tumour board [Q].
questions.merk: Primary RPLND for IIA/B seminoma: an alternative with conditions, not a standard; centre, selection, preferably a study.
questions.flag: No randomised data. NCCN (Version 2.2025) lists primary RPLND below 3 cm as an option; EAU 2026 restricts it to a study or cohort context. Reassess after PRIMETEST II results.

questions.objective: Can plan the template and approach for primary RPLND in seminoma according to the side of disease, preservation of function and centre expertise.
questions.vignette: A 28-year-old man with left-sided seminoma has a single 2.2 cm left para-aortic node and normal markers. The tumour board recommends primary RPLND; the centre has comparable experience with open and robotic surgery. The patient wants children and asks about preserving ejaculation. The operation must be planned.
questions.lead: Which operative plan is best supported?

opts.A: Bilateral template, because only this ensures radicality
opts.B: Robotic approach mandatory because it is oncologically superior
opts.C: Open approach mandatory because robotic surgery causes more relapses
opts.D: Unilateral template plus ipsilateral pelvic lymph node dissection
opts.E: Modified left-sided template, approach according to expertise

rat.A: Misconception: more resection means more safety. Bilateral templates were used only in some SEMS patients and showed no oncological advantage [Q].
rat.B: Misconception: technical advantages are oncological advantages. Robotic surgery showed less blood loss, shorter stay and better cosmetic results; randomised comparisons are lacking [Q].
rat.C: The opposite misconception. No oncological disadvantage of robotic surgery was demonstrated [Q]; both approaches are considered feasible and safe.
rat.D: Misconception: the radiotherapy field can be applied to surgery. Ipsilateral pelvic extension belongs to radiotherapy [Q]; the RPLND template follows retroperitoneal disease [Q].
rat.E: The modified unilateral template follows the side of radiologically demonstrated nodes and aims for tumour control with minimal loss of function [Q].

questions.core: The template follows the side of disease; the approach follows centre expertise. Both aim for maximal tumour control with minimal functional impairment.
questions.ev: The studies predominantly used a modified unilateral template; antegrade ejaculation was preserved in 94% in PRIMETEST, and bilateral templates showed no oncological advantage in SEMS [Q]. Open and robotic approaches are feasible and safe; a randomised comparison is lacking, and robotic RPLND requires appropriate expertise [Q].
questions.prax: For patients wanting children, discuss the residual risk of losing ejaculation and cryopreservation before surgery [X]. Without robotic experience, the open approach is the safe choice [Q].
questions.merk: Template according to disease side, approach according to expertise, not presumed oncological superiority.
questions.flag: Template and approach data come from single-arm phase II studies and a matched-pair analysis; randomised comparisons are lacking.

questions.objective: Can weigh the indication for one adjuvant cycle of BEP after primary RPLND using pathological risk markers.
questions.reference: Article: evidence, adjuvant treatment after RPLND; EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.1
questions.vignette: A 35-year-old man with stage IIB seminoma underwent primary RPLND. Histology: three involved nodes, largest lesion 2.4 cm, R0. Postoperative markers are normal and recovery is uncomplicated. He wants to reduce relapse risk but avoid unnecessary treatment. The tumour board must define postoperative management.
questions.lead: Which postoperative approach is best supported?

opts.A: Three cycles of BEP as for initially metastatic disease
opts.B: Offer one adjuvant cycle of BEP and weigh the benefit
opts.C: Two cycles of carboplatin AUC 7 as adjuvant monotherapy
opts.D: Adjuvant radiotherapy to the operative area with 30 Gy
opts.E: Follow-up without risk assessment because RPLND was curative

rat.A: Misconception: positive nodes require full metastatic-stage treatment. Only one adjuvant cycle of BEP was studied when risk markers were present [Q].
rat.B: More than two involved nodes are a risk marker; one cycle of BEP substantially reduced relapse in the Scandinavian study [Q].
rat.C: Misconception: applying the stage I carboplatin concept. After RPLND with risk markers, cisplatin-containing BEP was tested, not carboplatin [Q].
rat.D: Misconception: surgery and radiotherapy complement each other. Adjuvant approaches after primary RPLND are systemic [Q]; radiotherapy would negate the radiation-free approach [X].
rat.E: Misconception: no relevant relapse risk remains after R0 resection. Relapse-free survival after RPLND in the studies was 70–90% [Q]; risk markers change that risk.

questions.core: Three involved nodes meet a pathological risk criterion. A single adjuvant cycle of BEP then lowers relapse risk and must be weighed against the chance of avoiding chemotherapy entirely.
questions.ev: A multicentre Scandinavian study gave one adjuvant cycle of BEP for more than two positive nodes or nodes above 3 cm, substantially reducing relapse [Q]. The ongoing PRIMETEST II study examines which factors justify adjuvant treatment [Q]. EAU describes RPLND series with and without adjuvant chemotherapy [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.1] and considers all de-escalation strategies still under evaluation [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2].
questions.prax: The decision requires weighing options, not automatic treatment: without adjuvant therapy some patients remain chemotherapy-free, and relapse could be treated with chemotherapy [Q]. The pathology report must therefore explicitly state the number of involved nodes and the largest diameter [X].
questions.merk: After RPLND with risk markers—more than two positive nodes or nodes above 3 cm—consider one cycle of BEP, not three.
questions.flag: The risk criteria come from a population-based cohort and are not prospectively validated; PRIMETEST II is ongoing.

questions.objective: Can recognise relapse after primary RPLND as a chemotherapy-naive situation and treat according to stage.
questions.vignette: A 31-year-old man underwent primary left-sided RPLND without adjuvant therapy nine months ago for stage IIA seminoma. Follow-up CT shows a new 2.8 cm right paracaval node outside the template, with no other abnormality; AFP is normal and β-hCG mildly elevated. He has never received chemotherapy. Relapse treatment must be selected.

opts.A: First-line treatment according to IGCCCG, usually three cycles of BEP
opts.B: Salvage regimen with four cycles of TIP or alternatively VIP
opts.C: Repeat RPLND extended to a bilateral template
opts.D: Carboplatin AUC 7, then involved-node radiotherapy with 36 Gy
opts.E: Para-aortic and ipsilateral pelvic radiotherapy with 36 Gy

rat.A: The patient is chemotherapy-naive. Relapse after RPLND receives standard chemotherapy, which almost always cures according to EAU [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.1]; the studies achieved this in all relapses [Q].
rat.B: Misconception: salvage means second-line. TIP and VIP are intended for relapse after cisplatin-based first-line treatment [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.4]; this patient has not had chemotherapy.
rat.C: Misconception: applying the surgical relapse logic of nonseminoma. Chemotherapy is the supported approach for relapse after primary RPLND in seminoma [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.1].
rat.D: Misconception: de-escalation is also first choice at relapse. The combined regimen was tested as primary treatment in stage IIA/B, not after RPLND [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: after surgery radiotherapy is an equivalent local option. Standard chemotherapy is supported for relapse after RPLND [Q]; the source provides no radiotherapy data in this situation [X].

questions.core: Relapse after primary RPLND occurs in a chemotherapy-naive patient. He therefore receives stage-appropriate first-line chemotherapy, not a second-line salvage regimen.
questions.ev: In SEMS, COTRIMS and PRIMETEST all relapses were successfully treated with salvage chemotherapy [Q]. EAU states that relapse after primary RPLND is almost always cured by standard chemotherapy [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.1]; ifosfamide-containing combinations such as TIP or VIP are reserved for relapse after cisplatin-based first-line treatment [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.4]. BEP x 3 is standard for good prognosis [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.3.1.1].
questions.prax: In the RPLND context, salvage means rescue after surgery, not second-line. IGCCCG classification uses the findings at the time of relapse [X].
questions.merk: Relapse after primary RPLND: chemotherapy-naive, so first-line according to IGCCCG, usually three cycles of BEP.

questions.objective: Can distinguish the SAKK 01/10 regimen from conventional radiotherapy, stage I adjuvant treatment and SAKK 01/18.
questions.vignette: A 40-year-old man with stage IIA seminoma (single para-aortic node 1.7 cm, confirmed growth, normal markers, otherwise normal complete staging) is treated at a testicular cancer centre. Following a tumour board decision and counselling about the evidence, he is to receive de-escalated chemoradiotherapy according to SAKK 01/10. The treatment sequence must be defined.
questions.lead: How should treatment according to SAKK 01/10 be delivered?

opts.A: Involved-node radiotherapy, then one cycle of carboplatin AUC 7
opts.B: One cycle of carboplatin AUC 7, then a conventional dog-leg field
opts.C: One cycle of carboplatin AUC 7, then involved-node radiotherapy
opts.D: One cycle of etoposide and cisplatin, then involved-node 30 Gy
opts.E: Two cycles of carboplatin AUC 7 without subsequent radiotherapy

rat.A: Misconception: the sequence is arbitrary. One cycle of carboplatin followed by small-volume radiotherapy was tested [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2].
rat.B: Misconception: confusion with the British study combining carboplatin with conventional radiotherapy [Q]. SAKK 01/10 specifically reduces volume, to about one quarter on average [Q].
rat.C: One cycle of carboplatin AUC 7, then irradiation of involved nodes only with a small safety margin; in stage IIA, 30 Gy in 15 fractions [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2].
rat.D: Misconception: confusion with SAKK 01/18, which experimentally tests one cycle of etoposide and cisplatin in stage IIB; results are pending [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: applying stage I adjuvant treatment. Without irradiation of involved nodes, the local component of the tested regimen is missing [Q].

questions.core: SAKK 01/10 replaces high cumulative chemotherapy doses and large fields with a less intensive combination: first one cycle of carboplatin, then irradiation of involved nodes only [Q].
questions.ev: In the largest study of this type to date, 120 patients received one cycle of carboplatin AUC 7 followed by involved-node radiotherapy; the volume was about one quarter of the dog-leg field, and progression-free survival after at least 3 years was just under 94% [Q]. EAU specifies 30 Gy in 15 fractions for IIA and 36 Gy in 18 fractions for IIB, and a 3-year PFS of 93.7%, narrowly missing the primary endpoint of 95% [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2].
questions.prax: NCCN lists the regimen as an alternative [Q]; EAU does not yet consider it established for routine use [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2]. The indication belongs in a specialist centre's tumour board [Q].
questions.merk: SAKK 01/10: one cycle of carboplatin AUC 7, then involved-node radiotherapy; volume about one quarter of the dog-leg field.
questions.flag: Single-arm phase II study, primary endpoint narrowly missed; NCCN lists the regimen as an alternative, EAU 2026 does not support routine use.

questions.objective: Can provide a reasoned recommendation for standard chemotherapy over de-escalation concepts in larger stage IIB disease.
questions.reference: Article: standard treatments, radiotherapy, conclusions on RPLND; EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1 and 6.2.2.1.2
questions.vignette: A 36-year-old man with seminoma has a single 4.1 cm para-aortic node (stage IIB), normal markers and otherwise normal staging. He has read about combined carboplatin and radiotherapy and wants to avoid standard chemotherapy. No suitable study is open at the centre. Counselling precedes the treatment decision.
questions.lead: Which recommendation is best supported for this patient?

opts.A: Carboplatin plus involved-node radiotherapy as an equivalent approach
opts.B: One cycle of EP plus involved-node 30 Gy outside a study
opts.C: Primary RPLND with a bilateral template because of node size
opts.D: Three cycles of BEP; consider de-escalation only in a study context
opts.E: Para-aortic and pelvic radiotherapy with 36 Gy as the preferred choice

rat.A: Misconception: NCCN inclusion means equivalence. In SAKK 01/10, relapses occurred almost exclusively in stage IIB [Q]; EAU finds no evidence for routine use [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2].
rat.B: Misconception: a study concept is already clinical practice. SAKK 01/18 tests this modification for stage IIB; results are expected in 2026/2027 [Q].
rat.C: Misconception: a larger node justifies a larger template. NCCN lists primary RPLND only for nodes below 3 cm, and bilateral templates gave no oncological advantage [Q].
rat.D: Combination chemotherapy is preferred in stage IIB [Q]; according to EAU, de-escalation strategies belong in specialist centres with a study or prospective cohort [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2].
rat.E: Misconception: both standards have equal priority in stage IIB. Radiotherapy with 36 Gy is possible, but chemotherapy is preferred [Q]; EAU notes a nonsignificant efficacy trend in its favour [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1].

questions.core: With a node above 4 cm in stage IIB and no study option, chemotherapy is the best-supported choice [Q]. De-escalation concepts have their weakest support specifically in this group [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2].
questions.ev: Combination chemotherapy is preferred in stage IIB; more than 90% are cured by first-line treatment [Q]. EAU assigns all de-escalation strategies, including RPLND, to specialist centres with a study or prospective cohort [LL EAU 2026, 6.2.2.1.2].
questions.prax: The wish for de-escalation is legitimate but does not change the evidence: counselling covers both the late toxicity of chemotherapy and the insufficient support for alternatives [Q]. Referral to a centre with an open study remains possible [X].
questions.merk: Large IIB without a study: three cycles of BEP; de-escalation is least well supported here.
questions.flag: NCCN and EAU 2026 differ in their assessment of de-escalation; SAKK 01/18 results are expected in 2026/2027.
